title: Python Sets and Frozensets for NFA State Sets
description: Demonstrates set membership, deduplication, order independence, sorted printing, empty set creation, update with lists, and why frozenset is needed to store state sets inside another set.

steps.description: `active` is a set of two states. Line 2 prints three things: `"q0" in active` is `True`, `len({"q2", "q2"})` is `1` because sets deduplicate, and `{"q1", "q0"} == {"q0", "q1"}` is `True` because order does not matter. Line 3 shows `sorted` gives a consistent order and `{}` creates a `dict`, not a set.

`moved = set()` creates an empty set (not `{}`). Three `update` calls add items from lists: first `["q0"]`, then `["q0", "q2"]` (which adds `q2` and ignores the duplicate `q0`), then `[]` (which adds nothing). The print shows the sorted result `['q0', 'q2']`.
`closed = frozenset({"q0", "q1"})` makes an immutable set. It supports `in` and equality with regular sets, so `"q0" in closed` and `closed == {"q1", "q0"}` are both `True`.

steps.question: Line 16 tries `seen.add({"q0", "q1"})` where `seen` is a regular set. What happens?
steps.answer: A `TypeError: unhashable type: 'set'`. Regular sets are mutable, so Python cannot hash them and will not let them be elements of another set.

steps.description: The `except` catches the error and prints it. Then line 19 adds `frozenset({"q0", "q1"})` to `seen`, which works because frozensets are hashable. Line 20 checks membership with an equal frozenset and prints `True`.
Run it. Line 2 executes and prints `True 1 True`.
The `try` block raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'set'`, which the `except` prints.
The frozenset is added to `seen` successfully.
Membership test prints `True`. The frozenset with the same elements is found in `seen`.
